newsitem.title: USA: Miss. high court orders fresh hearing on Liggett.
newsitem.headline: Miss. high court orders fresh hearing on Liggett.

text.p: The Mississippi Supreme Court on Friday ordered a lower court judge to rehear arguments on whether documents from the Liggett Group should be released to plaintiffs in a $650 million wrongful death suit against cigarette makers.
The ruling put the decision back in the hands of Jones County Circuit Judge Billy Joe Landrum, the same judge who ordered the documents released to the family of the late Burl Butler on March 26.
Butler, who never smoked, died of cancer in 1994. His family alleges he was killed by second-hand smoke.
Tobacco industry attorneys persuaded the Mississippi high court to stay that release until Friday while they appealed Landrum's decision.

The Supreme Court judges found that a March 25 hearing in Jones County was conducted "without adequate or proper notice to all parties and without an opportunity for (the tobacco industry) to present argument and evidence regarding the delivery of the documents."
Last month's hearing, after which Landrum said 11 Liggett documents could be turned over to plaintiffs, was held with six days' notice.
An attorney for the Butler family said plaintiffs were not discouraged to have the document question back before Landrum.

"I am somewhat disappointed. But I am not discouraged. I am confident that we will have these documents in our possession in a short period of time. We are just going to have to wait a little longer," said attorney Cynthia Langston.

The Butler suit alleges that the tobacco industry knew about the dangers of smoking decades ago but concealed its own research. Over that time, Butler, a Laurel, Miss., barber, breathed in smoke from his patrons' cigarettes, cigars and pipes in his tiny shop.

The internal documents from Brooke Group Ltd's Liggett Group were released last month as part of a court settlement between the U.S. cigarette maker and 22 state attorneys general. The states are suing the tobacco industry for an estimated $30 billion in Medicaid funds spent to treat poor people for smoking-related illnesses.
The documents have been kept under seal since the settlement was announced.
Plaintiffs in the Butler case believe the documents show that cigarette makers destroyed information in order to hide it both from the public and plaintiffs in various lawsuits against the industry.
Attorneys for the tobacco industry on Friday were not immediately available to comment on the Supreme Court ruling.
